mainEntity.name: Can I have dental implants if I use a wheelchair?

acceptedAnswer.text: Using a wheelchair does not in itself prevent someone from having dental implants. Implant suitability is determined by factors such as bone quality and volume, general health, medication use, and oral hygiene capacity — not by mobility status. A thorough clinical assessment, including a discussion of your medical history and any relevant health conditions, will allow your dental team to advise on whether implants are a suitable option for you individually. Many wheelchair users undergo implant treatment with appropriate planning and personalised aftercare support.

mainEntity.name: How do I clean around a dental implant if I have limited hand dexterity?

acceptedAnswer.text: There are several adaptive tools that can make cleaning around a dental implant easier if you have limited grip strength or dexterity. Electric toothbrushes with large handles require minimal wrist movement and can clean effectively with gentle pressure. Water flossers direct a stream of water to clean between teeth and around the implant crown without requiring fine motor skills. Your dental team or an occupational therapist can advise on which tools are most appropriate for your specific circumstances and demonstrate correct technique.

mainEntity.name: What medications might affect my dental implant healing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Several medications can influence implant healing. Bisphosphonates, used for bone density conditions, can affect how bone responds to surgical procedures. Anticoagulants may influence bleeding and healing. Immunosuppressant medications can reduce the body's ability to manage infection. Many medications can also cause dry mouth, which reduces saliva's natural protective role in the mouth. It is important to provide your dental team with a full, up-to-date medication list and to inform them of any changes during treatment or the healing period.

mainEntity.name: What is peri-implantitis and how can I reduce the risk?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the gum and bone tissue surrounding a dental implant, caused by bacterial infection. It can lead to bone loss around the implant if not addressed. The risk can be reduced through consistent daily oral hygiene around the implant, regular professional dental cleaning, avoiding smoking, maintaining good systemic health, and attending all follow-up appointments. Early signs — such as redness, bleeding, or swelling around the implant — should be reported to your dental team promptly for assessment.

mainEntity.name: How often should I attend dental check-ups after having an implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your dental team will advise on a review schedule personalised to your situation, but in general, most implant patients benefit from at least twice-yearly check-ups and professional cleaning. Some patients — particularly those with systemic health conditions, a history of gum disease, or identified risk factors — may benefit from more frequent monitoring. Follow-up appointments allow your dental team to assess the health of the implant and surrounding tissues, provide professional maintenance, and identify any early concerns that can be addressed promptly.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if my dental implant feels loose or uncomfortable?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you notice that your implant crown or implant itself feels loose, uncomfortable, or different to usual, you should contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment as soon as possible. A feeling of looseness may indicate a problem with the crown fixation or, less commonly, with the implant itself. Prompt professional evaluation allows your dental team to investigate the cause and advise on the appropriate next steps. It is always better to seek assessment early rather than wait for a scheduled appointment in this situation.
